# Multilingual whitebox audit evaluation fixtures

These small, standalone Java, Python, and C source trees implement the fixture preparation in steps 6 and 11 of [the design](../../../../docs/multilang-whitebox-audit-design.md). They contain intentional flaws and nearby controls, plus test context for inventory classification. They use only language standard libraries and have no build manifests, listeners, executable entry points, compiled artifacts, or external dependencies. Select each language directory explicitly as a source audit root; these are not deployable service-discovery examples.

**No actual LLM audit evaluation was performed.** The expected results below are manually specified ground truth, not observed detections or measured A/B/C distributions. The Go regression checks collection, source reading, and production/test separation only. It does not compile, import, or execute these sources, call an LLM, validate candidate tiers, or prove vulnerability detection quality.

Use only source mode in an isolated, authorized local workspace with synthetic data and no production credentials. Never run exposed services from these fixtures or wrap the vulnerable functions in a network service. Evaluation needs source inspection only; do not execute vulnerable paths. Python and C binary auditing are outside this fixture set's scope. Budget defaults and policies are unchanged.

## Expected findings and controls

Paths below are relative to each language root. Marker comments provide stable anchors; line numbers describe this revision and must be refreshed from the actual file when constructing evidence. Cite real symbols and exact read lines, not just marker IDs. Each unsafe function represents one expected finding; multiple bad operations in that function are supporting anchors for that same finding.

| ID / language | Expected flaw and anchors | Nearby safe/control case | Required assumptions and reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| JAVA-AUTHZ / Java | `src/main/java/audit/NoteStore.java`, `readUnchecked`, line 18 (parameters), line 19 (`JAVA-AUTHZ-READ`); missing authorization, CWE-862 | `readOwned`, lines 22–27; ownership rejection at line 24 (`JAVA-AUTHZ-CONTROL`) | `principal` is a trusted authenticated identity, `noteId` is untrusted, and the trusted map holds notes owned by different users. Looking up a note without comparing its owner exposes another owner's note. The control denies absent notes and owner mismatches. Fixture owners are non-null; identity establishment and network reachability are not implemented. |
| PY-SQL / Python | `catalog.py`, `lookup_unchecked`, line 4 (parameters), line 6 (`PY-SQL-BUILD`), line 7 (`PY-SQL-EXECUTE`); SQL injection, CWE-89 | `lookup_bound`, lines 10–13; bound value at line 12 (`PY-SQL-CONTROL`) | A trusted SQLite connection has an `items(name)` table; `requested_name` is untrusted. The unsafe query interpolates it inside SQL quotes before executing, so it can alter the WHERE predicate. The control binds a value to a fixed query. No HTTP entry point is claimed. |
| C-COPY / C | `label.c`, `copy_unchecked`, lines 7–9; write at line 8 (`C-COPY-WRITE`) and terminator at line 9 (`C-COPY-TERMINATOR`); out-of-bounds write, CWE-787 | `copy_bounded`, lines 12–18; rejecting `len >= 16` at line 13 (`C-COPY-CONTROL`) | `label` points to 16 writable bytes, `src` to at least `len` readable bytes, the regions do not overlap, and `len` is untrusted. The array parameter does not enforce capacity. Length 16 already makes the terminator out of bounds; larger lengths can overflow the copy too. The control reserves one byte for NUL. This uses capacity/check/write reasoning, without requiring a process-execution sink or an invented call chain. |

Test-only context is `java/src/test/java/audit/NoteStoreTest.java`, `python/tests/test_catalog.py`, and `c/tests/label_test.c`. Each must be inventoried as `test`, remain available for contextual reading, and contribute zero production coverage files. Safe controls should produce no finding for the corresponding flaw under the stated assumptions. Reporting both C write sites separately is a duplicate, not a second expected flaw. Other supported claims require manual review rather than automatic rejection for using a different category label.

The corpus has three positive cases and three controls. Marker comments and descriptive names deliberately make these pedagogical examples easy; results do not estimate real-world detection accuracy. Keep this README and the Go expectations out of model input. Record whether source marker comments are visible, and keep that choice constant when comparing runs.

## A/B/C measurement procedure (not yet run)

1. Freeze the repository revision and fixture hashes. For each language, create a separate source-only audit with that directory as the explicit scope. Use an isolated evaluation workspace/database and synthetic data. Record model/provider/version, prompt revision, adapter, audit settings, coverage/final-sweep settings, retry policy, and run ID. Keep settings consistent across comparisons; do not change budget policy for this procedure. Record consumed tokens, completion status, and interruptions so incomplete runs remain distinguishable.
2. Let the existing source reader collect and read the production file and any needed test context. Save the actual read ranges, analyzed-file declarations, and coverage ledger. There is exactly one production file per root. Unread or unanalyzed production code is a coverage gap, not evidence of a clean audit. Collect all worker chunks and the final sweep where enabled.
3. Export every candidate submission, its canonical identity, validation issues, registration outcome, and retry/repair relationship. Use the platform's computed tier; do not ask the model to self-grade. **A** means complete supported evidence with no effective block and explicit exploitability conditions, registered with normal report queueing. **B** means real, read anchors with a soft evidence/chain/control/exploitability gap, registered at low confidence without automatic reporting. **C** means a hard evidence failure (for example unread lines, an out-of-scope file, a missing symbol or core anchor), retained as incomplete. Category spelling alone is not an accuracy criterion. Static registration never proves dynamic exploitation.
4. Per language and for the combined corpus, report A, B, and C counts and shares with an explicit denominator: tiered submissions `N = A + B + C`, with shares `A/N`, `B/N`, `C/N`. Count each submission/repair attempt in this view and also report the terminal tier per canonical candidate identity, so repair promotions do not inflate unique detections. Separate unclassified/parse-failed responses, empty responses, infrastructure failures, and interrupted runs from that denominator. If `N = 0`, shares are not applicable. Report validation-issue counts grouped by reason (and language); reasons can overlap and their percentages need not sum to 100%.
5. Measure duplicate submissions separately: among submissions carrying an identity, count each submission after the first occurrence of that identity and divide by identity-bearing submissions. Include chunk/sweep duplicates and report repair retries separately, so deliberate repair traffic is visible. Check that deduplication leaves at most one registered finding per expected flaw; also manually inspect semantic duplicates that used different identity keys. Count the two C write anchors as one issue.
6. Manually match candidates and registered findings to the three expected flaw IDs by behavior and anchors. For each language report whether its positive case was emitted at all and whether it reached A/B registration; a C-only candidate is not a registered detection. Review all three safe controls for false positives. Inspect every expected flaw that was absent or only C, distinguishing inventory/read/analysis gaps from model misses and validator rejection. Summarize positive-case recall (registered expected flaws / 3), control false positives (flagged controls / 3), coverage, duplicate rate, and rejection reasons alongside tier shares. A high A share alone is not an accuracy score. Preserve unsupported additional claims for manual adjudication.
7. Repeat the same fixed setup across the chosen models/settings or prompt revisions, recording the number of runs and variation. Save raw outputs and measurements outside these source fixture roots. Do not fill in observed scores until actual evaluations have run; the three expected positives are ground truth, not a promise that every submission will receive tier A.

## Focused inventory regression

From the repository root, run:

```sh
go test ./server -run '^TestTaskCodeAuditMultilangFixtureInventory$' -count=1
```

The regression uses the registered language adapter, real disk collector, production path/count helpers, and source reader for each root. It checks that exactly one production source and one test-context file are collected, that expected flaw/control anchors can be read, and that test context stays outside production paths/counts. No application launch or LLM call is required. The server package's shared `TestMain` may use configured PostgreSQL even for this focused test; point `ARTEX_PG_DSN` at an isolated test database or an unavailable local socket when running the inventory check.
